summary.text:
A district council that has funded its capital programme almost entirely from its own cash. At 31 March 2026 it held £21.6m of capital financing requirement against £4.0m of actual borrowing — all of it PWLB, all of it old, at an average 2.08% with 16.8 years to run. The gap is the story: £13.7m under-borrowed on the council's own prudential indicator, and £17.6m if finance leases are set aside.

That gap is currently profitable. The council earns 4.10% on £20.4m of investments while paying 2.08% on its debt, so internal borrowing is not a cost but a carry. The position is narrowing from both ends: investments fell £3.0m in the year and the return on them dropped from 4.34% to 4.10%, while the CFR rose £1.5m. No new borrowing was taken in 2025/26 and £0.858m was repaid.

The council has said when it intends to borrow. Its capital strategy states that as reserves and balances diminish over the life of the MTFS it will be necessary to draw new borrowing, and that external borrowing will likely be drawn once rates fall to around 5%. That is a stated trigger, not an inference — and PWLB is not there: the 5-year maturity rate fixed at 5.59% and the 10-year at 6.07% on 11 August 2026.

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on your 2025/26 treasury outturn. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

A cross-check first, and with a book your size it is exact. We hold both of your PWLB loans: £2m at 2.07% maturing 11 March 2070 and £2m at 2.08% maturing 11 March 2066. £4.000m, weighted 2.075% against the 2.08% you report.

We wrote because of the trigger. Your capital strategy says that as reserves and balances diminish over the life of the MTFS new borrowing will be needed, and that external borrowing will likely be drawn once rates fall to around 5%. That is a stated, published threshold, which is rarer than it sounds — most councils describe an intention rather than a number, and a number is something you can actually watch.

So: as at this afternoon's fixing, notice 314/26, one-year PWLB certainty is 4.95%. It is already through your threshold. Two-year is 5.06%, five-year 5.34% and ten-year 5.83%, so the long end is not there and is not especially close. Bank Rate is 3.75% and the market-implied path from SONIA has the one-year at 4.11% and two-year at 4.21%. Whether a trigger written as "around 5%" is meant to apply to the tenor you would actually borrow at is your call entirely and we have no view — but the answer today plainly depends on which point of the curve it attaches to, and that is worth having settled before the moment arrives rather than during it.

This is the thing we are actually built for. Rates fix twice daily and we publish both, with the forward curve and an implied Bank Rate path next to them, so a stated trigger becomes something the system watches rather than something someone remembers to check. It is free and it stays free.

The position behind the trigger is a good one and worth saying so. £21.6m of CFR against £4.0m of actual borrowing, £13.7m under-borrowed on your own prudential indicator and £17.6m setting finance leases aside. And it currently pays: you earn 4.10% on £20.4m of investments while paying 2.08% on the debt, so internal borrowing is carry rather than cost. It is narrowing from both ends though — investments down £3.0m in the year and their return down from 4.34% to 4.10%, CFR up £1.5m — which is presumably why the trigger is written down at all.

One thing from our side that is striking mainly for its proportion. Both your loans are around 2.07% with forty-odd years still to run, so on the DMO's premature repayment curve today they price about £2.2m below par between them — an indicative settlement of roughly £1.784m against £4.000m of principal, or about 45% of par. Nothing follows from that: we don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, only the DMO can quote, and with £4m outstanding it is an observation rather than an opportunity. We mention it because it is the clearest illustration we hold of what pre-2022 long money is now worth, and it is at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

For context on the market you would be borrowing into: July was £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02% — a thin month, and thin months matter more to a small borrower than a large one. That breakdown is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

On training, four fit Blaby. Reading the PWLBpredict and SONIA Forward Curve & OIS are the two that turn a 5% trigger into something monitored. Liability Benchmark: the essentials is the indicator that answers when the under-borrowing has to end. And PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator for the pricing above. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.
